<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:
Cluster was upgraded from 1.19.5 to 1.20.1 using kubeadm. After that, kube-apiserver cpu usage went from 50% to 300%.

**What you expected to happen**:
Expected that apiserver has the same cpu usage.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Update a cluster from 1.19.5 to 1.20.1.

**Anything else we need to know?**:
The cluster is running on sbc hardware, thats why the original 50% cpu usage, and thats why 300% cpu usage is noticeable and causes service disruption.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): (the apiserver is rolled back to 1.19.5)
```
$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"20", GitVersion:"v1.20.1", GitCommit:"c4d752765b3bbac2237bf87cf0b1c2e307844666", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2020-12-18T12:09:25Z", GoVersion:"go1.15.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"19", GitVersion:"v1.19.5", GitCommit:"e338cf2c6d297aa603b50ad3a301f761b4173aa6", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2020-12-09T11:10:32Z", GoVersion:"go1.15.2", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/arm"}
```
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
bare metal on SBC hardware.
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`):

- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug):

- Others:
Please check profiling of each apiserver.
[apiserver.tar.gz](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/5764262/apiserver.tar.gz)

So, apiserver behavior is a bit random regarding this issue. What is true that on my hardware (orange pi pc) the apiserver needs around 85 cpu seconds to boot up, after that it consumes ~10% cpu time. When a build is bad, apiserver passes the 85 cpu seconds and still uses more cpu than 10%, sometimes even 300%. So, based on this, bisecting shows 0809220fd04d26892f0fcfd3bf54cc4baeda22da is first bad commit.
Reverting that commit on 1.20.1 makes apiserver behaving as before. Consistently it finishes its bootup in 90 seconds, and then cpu usage gets to its normal 10-50%, it depends on load-balancer.

By the way, the problem is not just high cpu usage, but during bootup and high cpu usage, apiserver stays in not ready state, thus kubelet restarts it after failed liveness probes. So it may cause service outage.

> By the way, the problem is not just high cpu usage, but during bootup and high cpu usage, apiserver stays in not ready state, thus kubelet restarts it after failed liveness probes. So it may cause service outage.

I suspect, that the mentioned commit fixes things in a way that it actually places more cpu load, I mean https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/metrics/sample_and_watermark.go#L204 expression evaluates to true more often. The attached profiling data may be a proof for this.

It seems that on slower hardware, operations are distributed into more sample periods (time.Millisecond), which makes more calls to the expensive metrics.Observe functions. Before the mentioned fix, due to quantization bug, those calls were not made every time.Milliseconds. Now they are, and profiling data proves this. Can we raise the samplePeriod, can it be made configurable?

> Can we raise the samplePeriod, can it be made configurable?

sig api machinery can provide feedback on this.

> Before the mentioned fix, due to quantization bug, those calls were not made every time.Milliseconds.

is that accurate? my reading of the fix is that the quantize method returns results with the same granularity. The bug that was fixed was that quantization could return numbers that resulted in negative calculations if wall clock time changed, and now it respects the monotonic clock.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/96530/files#diff-550e44ca986c3a38068378ac63dca6bc182b1626b920ae87161c1195ebc71100L93

@liggitt Perhaps not. That was just my assumption. But still, profiling data shows (at least for me) that metric.Observe calls take most of the time, while reverting the mentioned commit solves my problem. Somehow less calls are made to them.
/assign @MikeSpreitzer

We have numerous K3s users reporting perf issues (and crashes in the cronjob controller) on armv7l. I can reproduce it locally on my Pi nodes as well. I hadn't gotten around to digging into it yet, so I'm glad someone else has done so.

We also had issues getting arm to build properly starting with Kubernetes 1.19.4; some builds would crash with what looked like a corrupted stack on armv7l unless we set `GOARCH="arm" GOARM="7"` for the build. See: https://github.com/k3s-io/k3s/issues/2535

Prior to doing that it was fairly random if a build would work or not; changing unrelated bits of code (ie bumping a vendored module version) would give us a clean build, and then changing something else would break it, and then changing a 3rd thing would give us a clean build again. It felt very much like golang arm toolchain issues. This sounds similar to what @rkojedzinszky reported with good vs bad builds.
